processing: Processed as a green tea, with heat fixing to stop oxidation. What sets it apart happens on the bush: a light-sensitive mutation makes the new shoots yellow.
harvest_season: New shoots stay yellow in spring, summer and autumn, so three seasons can yield fine tea; spring is the usual choice for green tea drinkers.
appearance_dry: Strikingly golden-yellow buds and leaves, far paler than ordinary green tea.
appearance_liquor: Typically a very pale, clear yellow-green.
appearance_wet: Soft yellow shoots that keep their golden tone.
taste_profile: Tasting notes vary by maker; like other low-chlorophyll yellow-leaf teas it is generally valued for a soft, sweet, savoury mouth with little bitterness.

brewing.notes: Typical for tender albino-type greens: cooler water protects the sweetness. Glass lets you enjoy the colour.

vintage_note: Sold as a current-year green tea, usually with the harvest season stated. Because it can also be picked later in the year, check that you are buying spring tea if that is what you want. Now grown beyond Zhejiang, so the place of origin matters as well as the name.
description:
Huangjinya, golden bud, is a tea cultivar before it is a tea: a natural mutation found around Yuyao near Ningbo, whose new shoots grow yellow instead of green. Despite the colour it is a green tea, not a yellow tea, which has its own separate processing.

The yellowing responds to light, and it holds through spring, summer and autumn flushes. That gives growers more than one season of fine tea and gives the dry leaf its look.

As with other yellow-leaf and albino-type cultivars, people usually look for softness, sweetness and savour rather than bite. Cooler water and a glass are the natural choice, because half the pleasure is looking at it.

The name now travels: Guangde in Anhui holds a registered geographical mark for its Huangjinya, and Guizhou sells it too. These are the same idea grown in different places, so read the label for origin.

Do not confuse the cultivar with old poetry: a Yuan-dynasty poem on Long Jing by Yu Ji uses the words huang jin ya as a figure of speech, long before this plant existed.
history:
Accounts of the discovery differ. A Ningbo research team's account dates the find to 1998, near the Tianluoshan site in Yuyao, while a consumer article credits Zhang Wanlin, head of a tea farm in Yuyao, with noticing it in the 1990s.

Ningbo reports yellow cultivars bred there spreading to more than twenty provinces.
